sections.heading: Sport as a mirror of society
sections.specBullet: The characteristics of pre-industrial Britain

paragraphs: Sport is often said to reflect the wider society it takes place in, so studying popular recreation before 1780 shows where modern sport came from. Five features of pre-industrial Britain shaped what sport could possibly look like.

rows: Most people lived and worked on the land, so activities took place on open fields, commons and village streets
Activities stayed local and varied from one area to another
Widespread illiteracy among the lower classes
Few written rules existed for games
A clearly divided, two-tier class system
An upper class with significant leisure time and wealth, and a lower or working class with very little free time, dictated by agricultural and seasonal demands
Long working hours and hard living conditions left little time or energy for sport, and were mirrored in how violent and physically demanding many activities were

items.meaning: The rigid structure society operated under, based on land ownership, where land was exchanged for labour or service. It reinforced a strict divide between the classes.

sections.heading: Popular recreation
sections.specBullet: The characteristics of popular recreation

items.meaning: The sport and leisure activities of the pre-industrial period, which reflected the conditions of the time: typically local and inconsistent between areas, played to few or no agreed rules, held infrequently and often tied to religious festivals or holidays, and sometimes aggressive, violent or disorderly, occasionally involving heavy gambling.

items: Local, because nobody could travel far
Few rules, because few people could write them down
Infrequent, because free time came only with festivals and holidays

sections.heading: Two contrasting examples
sections.specBullet: Mob football and real tennis as examples of popular recreation

items.meaning: An unruly, often violent form of football played by the lower classes with little formal structure, using local streets or fields, and frequently causing damage or injury. It was eventually banned in many areas.

An exclusive, skilful racket-and-ball sport played by the upper classes on purpose-built courts, requiring expensive equipment only the wealthy could access, and played with far more restraint and rule-following than mob football.

rows: Expensive, so only the wealthy could access it
Unruly and often violent, causing damage or injury, and eventually banned in many areas

paragraphs: The pairing is the point. The same society produced both, and the difference between them is a difference of class rather than of sport: time, money and space decided what each group could play.

sections.heading: The move towards rational recreation
sections.specBullet: The development of rational recreation

items.meaning: Sport that was more logically structured, better regulated by clear rules and less violent than earlier popular recreation. It reflected the more ordered, industrial society developing at the time.

Founded in 1850, and regarded as an important forerunner of the modern Olympics. It combined physical and intellectual competition, welcomed a wide range of social classes, and promoted the health and educational benefits of exercise.
Founder of the Wenlock Olympian Games, who also campaigned for physical education to be part of the school curriculum.
Influenced by Brookes's ideas after visiting the Wenlock Olympian Society in 1890. He went on to found the International Olympic Committee and revive the modern Olympic Games.
Founded by de Coubertin, who revived the modern Olympic Games in Athens in 1896.

items: 1850: Dr William Penny Brookes founds the Wenlock Olympian Games, mixing physical and intellectual competition across social classes
Brookes campaigns for physical education to be part of the school curriculum
1890: Baron Pierre de Coubertin visits the Wenlock Olympian Society and takes up the ideas
De Coubertin founds the International Olympic Committee
1896: the modern Olympic Games are revived in Athens

sections.heading: Social and cultural influences of the Industrial Revolution
sections.specBullet: The impact of the Industrial Revolution on sport

items.meaning: The transformation of Britain, roughly from the mid-eighteenth to the mid-nineteenth century, from a rural, agricultural society into an urban, industrial, factory-based one.

paragraphs: The effect on sport came in two waves. Early industrialisation made sport harder in almost every way, and only as conditions improved did the same forces begin to support it.

items.meaning: Poor health and hygiene in overcrowded factory towns.
Low wages left little money for leisure.
Long factory shifts left little time for recreation.
Open land used for traditional games was built over.
The festivals popular recreation had relied on were reduced, partly due to religious restrictions on Sunday activity.
New laws restricted or banned traditional mob games and blood sports.
Health and hygiene improved as living and working conditions gradually got better.
Workers had more money available for leisure.
Factory owners began organising and sponsoring works sports teams.
Travelling to play or to watch sport became cheaper and easier.

items: Early and negative: health, income, time, facilities, old traditions and holidays, rights
Later and positive: improved health, increased income, patronage, better transport
Health, income and time appear on both lists, because the same factors reversed

sections.heading: Urbanisation and communications
sections.specBullet: Urbanisation, transport and communications

items.meaning: The large-scale movement of people from the countryside into towns and cities to work in factories during the Industrial Revolution.

paragraphs: Towns filling up quickly put a large audience in one place, which is precisely what spectator sport needs. It also created demand for venues built for the purpose, because open ground had been built over and the sprawling games of the past had nowhere left to happen.

Improvements to transport, particularly the railway network, let teams and spectators travel further and more easily. That made regular fixtures between towns possible, along with national leagues and cup competitions, and cheaper travel widened access for the working classes. Alongside this, improved literacy and the printed media, such as newspapers, publicised fixtures and results more widely, which supported the growth of organised, national sport.

sections.heading: The Church and the middle classes
sections.specBullet: The influence of the Church and the middle classes

items.meaning: During the Victorian era the Church took an increasingly active role in promoting sport as a form of social control, encouraging behaviour it viewed as respectable and steering people away from activities such as heavy drinking and gambling.
A newly emerging class created by industrialisation and urbanisation, which became increasingly influential in organising sport.

paragraphs: The Church backed this up practically, opening its halls and playing fields to community clubs and encouraging clergy to organise sport themselves. Several football clubs, Aston Villa and Everton among them, were originally founded by church groups.

items.meaning: Writing down and standardising rules, and forming national governing bodies to administer them.
Organising formal leagues and cup competitions.
Developing facilities such as parks and public baths, often funded by wealthy philanthropists.
New legislation, such as the Factory Acts, introduced Saturday half-days, giving workers more time to play or watch sport.

paragraphs: These developments also drove early professionalism. Once sport was organised, regular and watched, agents, promoters and employers saw its commercial potential and began paying performers.

sections.heading: Sport and the British Empire
sections.specBullet: The spread of sport through the British Empire

paragraphs: Through the nineteenth century, English public schools were a major route by which sport reached the Empire. They treated it as a way of instilling discipline and moral values, and as something capable of binding people across the Empire together. The young men they educated then carried those sporting traditions abroad, whatever work they took up.

rows: Used sport as part of missionary work
Played and spread sport wherever they were stationed
Spread sporting values as they travelled

paragraphs: The lasting effect was on the rules. Codes written by British national governing bodies spread with the people who carried the games, and were adopted internationally as those sports took hold across former colonies.

sections.heading: Public provision and national governing bodies
sections.specBullet: Public provision and the emergence of national governing bodies

items.meaning: Facilities funded by local authorities for community use, such as public baths and parks. It developed particularly from the mid-nineteenth century, encouraged by legislation such as the Baths and Wash Houses Act 1846, improving public health while creating more recreational opportunities for the working classes.

Organisations set up to administer and regulate a sport nationally. They began to emerge from the mid-nineteenth century, the Football Association in 1863 among them, as participation became increasingly widespread and organised.

paragraphs: NGBs were formed for three reasons: to establish a single, agreed set of rules so different clubs could compete fairly; to organise leagues, fixtures and international competition; and, particularly among the upper and middle classes, to protect the amateur ideal by controlling or restricting professional involvement in a sport.

sections.heading: Characteristics of rational recreation
sections.specBullet: The characteristics of rational recreation

items.meaning: Non-violent, and played with an emphasis on fair play.
Fixtures played on a structured, ongoing basis rather than as one-off local events.
Governed by clear, standardised, codified rules.
Officials present to enforce the rules.
Administered through newly formed national governing bodies.
Reflecting the limited space and large populations of urban areas.
Play increasingly involved specific skills and tactical positions, rather than the disorganised mass participation of earlier popular recreation.

rows: Respectable, with officials to enforce fair play

sections.heading: Amateurism and professionalism
sections.specBullet: Amateurism and professionalism in the nineteenth century

items.meaning: Playing purely for enjoyment, with no payment.
Playing sport in return for financial reward.

paragraphs: Both codes ran alongside each other through the nineteenth century. The gentleman amateur ideal prized manliness and physical endurance, high moral integrity, a regard for health and fitness, and playing for the enjoyment of it rather than to win at any cost. It belonged to the wealthy, public-school-educated upper and middle classes, who could afford the time to compete without being paid for it.

rows: High standards of sportsmanship, honesty and fair play, since accepting money was seen as breaking the moral code. Many sports and governing bodies stayed under the control of the socially privileged, who viewed themselves as holding naturally higher status than professionals

Working-class players who could not afford to compete unpaid were excluded, and existing class divisions were reinforced, since some amateurs viewed themselves as superior to working-class professionals

paragraphs: Early working-class professionals, in rugby league for example, were in a very different position. They had far less free time and money, often relied on broken-time payments to cover wages lost while playing, and needed sport to be financially sustainable, which could create pressure to prioritise winning over strict amateur ideals.

items: Amateurism was a moral code and a class marker at the same time
Broken-time payments compensated lost wages, not performance
The ideals and the exclusion are two sides of the same rule

sections.heading: Amateurism and professionalism since 1900
sections.specBullet: The changing status of amateurism and professionalism

paragraphs: Amateurs were still the prominent figures early in the twentieth century, and socially they outranked professionals. They tended to come from privileged, financially secure backgrounds, and they frequently ran the national governing bodies themselves. That gap closed slowly across the decades, until what counted was what a performer could do rather than where they had come from.

In modern sport the word amateur has become blurred. Many top-level amateurs receive significant financial support for training, through National Lottery or Sports Aid funding, which raises the question of whether they are genuinely amateur at all, while some traditionally amateur sports still have lower-status, unpaid participation even at the top level.

Elements of the amateur code have survived into professional sport: Fair Play awards, pre-match and post-match handshakes, and the continued use of honorary titles in some sports linked to their amateur heritage.

rows: All social classes can now compete
Talent is no longer filtered by who can afford to play unpaid
Higher financial rewards and respect, through sponsorship and media coverage
Sport became a viable career rather than a pastime
More free time for full-time training
Celebrity culture and greater investment in sport
Professionals are funded, and audiences are motivated to follow elite competition

sections.heading: Association football
sections.specBullet: The rationalisation and modern development of association football

rows: Large concentrated audiences, and demand for purpose-built stadiums
More free time and disposable income among the working classes
The Saturday half-day became the traditional time for matches
Legalised in England in 1885, once it was clear many players were already being paid unofficially

paragraphs: The game became more organised alongside this: the Football Association formed in 1863, national rules were codified, and referees took control of officiating as football became increasingly commercialised.

items.meaning: A 1995 European Court of Justice decision giving out-of-contract players freedom of movement between clubs. It significantly increased player bargaining power and wages.

paragraphs: Women's football has grown a great deal, in professionalism and in popularity. Sex discrimination legislation gave it legal protection, the Women's Super League and the FIFA Women's World Cup gave it a media platform, and the FA has put funding and investment behind it. Grassroots opportunities have widened, and there are now visible role models playing, coaching and officiating.

Opportunities for female match officials historically lagged behind the men's game, but structured pathways have since been introduced to progress officials through league levels up to international level.

sections.heading: Lawn tennis
sections.specBullet: The rationalisation and modern development of lawn tennis

paragraphs: Lawn tennis was invented by the middle classes in the 1870s, patented by Major Walter Clopton Wingfield in 1874, as a more accessible, suburban alternative to real tennis. It was originally played on courts built in private gardens.

rows: Standardised written rules from the outset
A rational sport from the start, unlike popular recreation
Played in a socially exclusive and polite manner
Access was controlled by class, not by skill
Gradually opened up through public provision, such as courts built in public parks
Access widened beyond the middle classes

paragraphs: Tennis offered relatively early opportunities for women to take part, from the 1880s, which helped challenge some contemporary stereotypes about female participation, although women initially had to play in restrictive clothing.

sections.heading: Track and field athletics
sections.specBullet: The rationalisation and modern development of track and field athletics

paragraphs: Athletics rationalised alongside everything else, and for the same reason: towns were growing. Competition moved off open rural land and into venues built for it, which could hold a large crowd and charge it for entry.

items.meaning: Formed in 1880. It initially enforced a strict exclusion clause separating wealthier amateur athletes from those who competed for money, which excluded professional or manual-working competitors from amateur events.

paragraphs: Women's participation was historically very restricted. Women were not permitted to compete in Olympic athletics until 1928, and were excluded from longer-distance events such as the marathon at Olympic level until 1984.

Modern athletics is governed internationally by the sport's world governing body, which organises major events and coordinates funding. That allows elite athletes to train and compete full-time as professionals, supported by sponsorship, prize money and media coverage.

items: 1880 AAA and its exclusion clause: amateurism used to keep the working class out
1928 women admitted to Olympic athletics, 1984 for the marathon
Urban growth moved athletics from open land to paying stadiums

sections.heading: Commercialism, media and sponsorship
sections.specBullet: The golden triangle of sport, sponsorship and the media

items.meaning: The close, mutually dependent relationship between sport, business and sponsorship, and the media. Each part relies on and benefits the other two.
The process by which sport is increasingly run and promoted with the aim of generating profit, rather than purely for participation or enjoyment.

columns: What it needs from the others
rows: Media coverage and sponsorship, to grow and to fund performers
Popular sport, to attract viewers and advertising revenue

paragraphs: Modern commercial sport shares a recognisable set of features: high standards of skill and performance, close links between sponsorship and business, a strong entertainment focus, valuable contracts and merchandising deals, treatment of top athletes as marketable commodities and role models, and media coverage that is easy for a general audience to follow.

rows: Significant income from participation, sponsorship and merchandising, and greater financial security
Increased pressure to perform and win consistently, the need to specialise fully and often at the cost of privacy, and reduced personal control over their own public image

paragraphs: Commercialisation has directly changed the rules and presentation of some sports to make them more attractive to broadcasters and sponsors: shorter formats designed for television such as Twenty20 cricket, scoring changes to reduce time-wasting as in badminton, and breaks built into play for advertising.

The rise of television rights transformed the finances of major sports from the mid-twentieth century. English football has been broadcast since 1937, and the value of live TV rights grew from hundreds of millions to billions of pounds by the 2010s, giving broadcasters increasing influence over how and when events are staged.

Coverage and sponsorship have always flowed more freely towards men's sport. That ties back to lower participation, a shortage of visible role models, and less money being put back in at both grassroots and elite level. The position has improved markedly in recent years, on coverage and on investment alike.

Social media has since rearranged the relationship between sport, its fans and the traditional press. A club or a performer can speak to an audience directly now and build a following of their own, without needing print or broadcast to carry them. The trade-off is exposure: conduct online carries a reputational risk that did not previously exist.

sections.heading: The sociology of sport
sections.specBullet: Sociological theory applied to equal opportunities

paragraphs: Sociology asks how living in a society shapes and regulates the way people behave. Two questions sit at its centre: how people within a group interact with and depend on one another, and how their behaviour comes to be controlled, whether by family, by friends, by schools or by other institutions.

The sociology of sport applies those ideas to the relationship between sport and society, looking at how social processes such as socialisation can create or worsen inequalities for particular groups, including women, disabled people and ethnic minority groups.

sections.heading: Socialisation
sections.specBullet: Primary and secondary socialisation

items.meaning: A lifelong process through which a person learns and takes on the norms, values, attitudes and expected roles of the society or group they belong to.

Happens during early childhood, mainly within the immediate family of parents and siblings. Close, everyday contact strongly shapes early habits, including introducing children to physical activity and play, and can be a key influence on lifelong sporting participation.

Happens later, typically during the teenage years, once influence widens beyond the immediate family to include friends, school and wider social groups. Schools in particular play a major role by structuring young people's exposure to sport and PE.

sections.heading: Social control and social change
sections.specBullet: Sport as a tool of social control and social change

items.meaning: The way a society regulates people's thoughts, feelings, appearance and behaviour, keeping them in line with accepted norms. It is enforced both informally, by family and friends, and formally, by institutions such as schools, religious bodies or government bodies.

An alteration in the established order of society. Sporting campaigns and initiatives can be deliberately used to promote positive social change, such as increasing participation among a specific under-represented group.

paragraphs: Sport can act as a tool of social control: taking part in organised, rule-governed activity limits the opportunity to become involved in antisocial behaviour, and participation tends to be lower among groups with less access to organised, monitored activity.
Moving quickly is rarely possible. Differences in influence and access between groups run deep, and they carry on determining who actually takes part long after a campaign has started.

sections.heading: Causes of social inequality in sport
sections.specBullet: Social inequality and its causes

items.meaning: Where resources, opportunities and status within a society are unevenly shared out among different social groups.

paragraphs: In sport, inequality can be linked both to a person's economic position, meaning income and wealth, and to socially constructed differences based on characteristics such as gender, ethnicity or disability.

items.meaning: The cost of equipment, membership and travel can restrict participation.
A lack of visible, relatable role models to aspire to.
Harmful stereotypes about the ability of certain groups, based on ethnicity, gender or disability.
Low self-esteem or a lack of confidence discouraging people from taking part.

paragraphs: These barriers particularly affect women, disabled people, ethnic minority groups, and those from lower-income or unemployed households.

items: Four causes: money, role models, myths, confidence
Two of the four are about what people can afford, two about what they believe is possible
Inequality is economic and socially constructed at the same time

sections.heading: Social structures and stratification
sections.specBullet: Social stratification and social class

items.meaning: A form of inequality in which a society is divided into different layers or classes based on a shared characteristic, most commonly wealth or status.

paragraphs: A society's structure is shaped by a range of social factors that can positively or negatively affect an individual's or group's life chances. Sport participation has historically reflected that stratification: access to facilities and equipment has traditionally favoured wealthier groups, while lower-income groups have had more limited access.

In modern society, taking part in sport can be a way of gaining status and a sense of identity within a social group, though that status is usually temporary and specific to the sporting context, fading once the activity has ended.

Influence and visibility across sport still concentrate among the groups that have traditionally held power and wealth, which leaves everyone else thinly represented as participants, as coaches and in leadership. Class tracks participation closely. Equipment, coaching and travel all cost money, so children from lower-income households get less access from the start, and schools serving less affluent areas often have thinner facilities than fee-paying ones.

sections.heading: Social action theory and related terms
sections.specBullet: Social action theory, prejudice, discrimination and stereotyping

items.meaning: Views society and behaviour, including participation in sport, as something actively produced through the relationships and interactions between people, rather than something fixed. Individuals interpret situations and respond to one another, and this can gradually drive wider social change.
Gradual movement towards a more developed or advanced state, such as a steady rise in participation for an under-represented group over time.
Giving everyone the same chance to take part in an activity, regardless of characteristics such as race, sex, religion or mental and physical ability.
An unfair opinion or attitude formed about a person or group, often based on limited or inaccurate information rather than direct experience.
The unfair treatment of a person or group, usually resulting from prejudice, where they are treated differently or excluded because of a particular characteristic.
Applying a fixed, oversimplified assumption to every member of a group, which can unfairly limit how people from that group are viewed or treated in sport.

rows: Open racist abuse of a player
Quietly overlooking someone for a leadership role because of their background

items.wrong: Prejudice and discrimination are the same thing.
items.right: Prejudice is the attitude; discrimination is the action that usually results from it. Someone can hold a prejudice without acting on it.

sections.heading: Benefits of increasing participation
sections.specBullet: The benefits of increased participation for the individual and for society

rows: Improved fitness, weight management, lower blood pressure and reduced stress
Reduced pressure on health services and lower obesity-related illness
Stronger friendships and social skills from being part of a team or club
A constructive use of free time
Reduced criminal activity and lower resulting costs
A more active, healthier workforce overall
Increased spending on sport-related goods, services and jobs, boosting local and national income

paragraphs: Physiologically, regular activity builds almost every component of fitness: cardiovascular fitness, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility, agility, balance, coordination, speed, power and reaction time. It also lowers the likelihood of developing heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis and certain cancers.

Part of the explanation for better mood and lower stress is chemical: exercise releases serotonin and endorphins, which in turn tend to improve sleep, concentration and relationships with other people.

sections.heading: Barriers to participation and possible solutions
sections.specBullet: General barriers to participation and strategies to overcome them

items.meaning: Competing demands from work, study or family commitments.
The cost of equipment, membership and travel.
A lack of confidence or drive to get started.
Limited knowledge, skill or awareness of how to get involved.

paragraphs: The practical solutions answer each barrier in turn: build activity into an existing daily routine, such as walking or cycling to work or school; exercise with friends or family for motivation and support; offer low-cost or free sessions where facility access is limited; and choose simple activities that require minimal skill, cost or equipment.
The groups most affected by these barriers, and specifically targeted for increased participation, are women, disabled people, and people from minority ethnic groups.

items: Four barriers: time, income, motivation, education
Each barrier has a matching solution, so name the barrier first
Three target groups: women, disabled people, minority ethnic groups

sections.heading: Barriers facing disabled people
sections.specBullet: Barriers and solutions for disabled people

paragraphs: Participation rates among disabled people are lower than the general population, and recent data has shown a decline in the number of disabled people taking part in regular weekly exercise.

Several barriers recur. Self-image and confidence are often low. Income is often lower too, which makes membership fees and transport harder to meet. Facilities are frequently inaccessible, and there may be no adapted programmes or specialist coaches to go to. Media coverage is sparse, so relatable role models are scarce. Underneath all of it sit myths and stereotypes about what a disabled person is capable of.

rows: Openly excluding a disabled person from taking part
Quietly failing to adapt coaching or provision to include them
Disabled and non-disabled people taking part together
Disabled people competing separately among themselves, as at the Paralympics

paragraphs: Solutions include creating opportunities for elite success, such as the Paralympics; investing in accessible facilities, transport and assistive technology such as sport-specific wheelchairs and prosthetics; increasing media coverage and role models; training specialist coaches; designing inclusive, sport-specific activities; and educating the public to break down myths and stereotypes.

sections.heading: Barriers facing ethnic minority groups
sections.specBullet: Barriers and solutions for ethnic minority groups

items.meaning: The unfair or hostile treatment of a person based on their skin colour, language or cultural background. It is illegal in Britain.
The disproportionate concentration of ethnic minority players in certain playing positions, based on stereotypical assumptions about their physical rather than decision-making abilities.
Ethnic minority groups being steered towards or away from particular sports based on assumptions about their suitability.

paragraphs: The recurring barriers start with fear of being racially abused or rejected, and the low self-esteem that can follow from it. Role models and coaches from the same background are often absent. Cultural or religious observance can rule out particular settings, language can be an obstacle in itself, and stereotyping or outright discrimination shapes selection, coaching and employment.

Participation in physical activity runs below average in some ethnic minority communities. The gap widens away from the pitch: representation in coaching, management and administration falls well short of representation among players.

The responses work on several fronts: bringing through more coaches, officials and teachers from ethnic minority backgrounds; running culturally sensitive sessions where that is needed; making racist abuse public and punishing it; building a range of cultural practices into PE programmes; and campaigning against racism head-on. Some governing bodies go further, requiring that minority ethnic candidates be interviewed for certain coaching vacancies, so that leadership starts to reflect the people playing.

items.wrong: Stacking and channelling describe the same thing.
items.right: Stacking is about position within a sport. Channelling is about which sport a person is pushed towards in the first place.

sections.heading: Barriers facing women
sections.specBullet: Barriers and solutions for women

paragraphs: Women's participation in sport remains lower than men's, and is affected by a combination of stereotyping and discrimination.

items.meaning: Often reduced by childcare or domestic responsibilities.
A lack of visible, relatable women in sport.
Lower disposable income limiting access.
More limited choice and opportunity for girls at school.
Far less funding and investment compared with men's sport.

paragraphs: On top of these there is historically low media coverage of women's sport, fewer available leagues and clubs, and stereotypical views about what counts as an appropriately feminine sport, which can discourage participation in more traditionally masculine ones.

What helps: giving girls genuinely equal choice in school PE, enforcing equal treatment through sex discrimination law, putting women's sport on screen and promoting the role models that creates, designing flexible and sociable formats that fit around other commitments, improving access to childcare, and raising sponsorship and prize money for women's competitions. Sport England's This Girl Can was aimed squarely at these barriers, and participation and investment in women's sport have climbed steadily alongside it.

items: Five barriers: time, role models, income, PE programmes, sponsorship
Time here means childcare and domestic responsibility, not just a busy diary
Low coverage, low sponsorship and few role models reinforce each other

sections.heading: Sport England and its partners
sections.specBullet: Organisations working to increase participation

paragraphs: Sport England works with a range of local and national partners to increase participation and reduce inequality, with a stated mission of helping people build a lasting sporting habit for life.

items.meaning: Focused on increasing physical activity among disabled people.
Works to increase participation among disadvantaged and black and minority ethnic communities.
Aims to get more women and girls active, and to challenge the barriers to their participation.
Supports low-cost, informal doorstep sport in disadvantaged communities, close to where people live.

rows: A local pilot to increase women's activity
Facility investment, including for disabled people
